transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Li (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Redwood Solutions), Marcus Nguyen (ApolloPay CFO), Sofia Alvarez (ApolloPay Lead ML), Ben Carter (ApolloPay Eng Manager), Lina Xu (ApolloPay SRE)

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we will do a quick econ review then go into the bench results and tuning notes. Marcus, Sofia, Ben — you good on time?
[00:07] Marcus: Yep, all good. We got 45 minutes.
[00:10] Connor: Cool, Ill share my screen in a second — theres a spreadsheet link in the chat with the recent runs.
[00:18] Sofia: I saw that, thanks. Quick ask up front, were most concerned about tokens per dollar for our risk-scoring flow — short prompts but high QPS. Latency target is ~250-400ms p95.
[00:28] Aisha: Got it. That made sense from last week. Today well focus on tokens/sec per dollar, and the two levers we tried: prefix/KV caching and batching. We also ran a quantization pass on the 13B variant.
[00:38] Ben: Quick clarifying question — when you say prefix cache are we talking full KV cache across the session or just prompt prefix caching?
[00:45] Connor: Good question. For this experiment we enabled prefix caching for the static policy prompts — so the first 80 tokens are cached as KV and reused on subsequent requests. It's not session KV across different users, more like route-level prefix caching. The term in the logs is K V cache but yeah it's the usual KV cache.
[00:58] [01:05] Marcus: And how much did that save in the run? Numbers matter.
[01:08] Connor: So baseline hosted run (no caching, batch size 1) gave us about 2,100 tokens/sec per dollar on the request mix. With prefix caching enabled we saw up to 28% reduction in token compute per request for that route, which translated to roughly 18% tokens/sec per dollar improvement overall across the pilot traffic.
[01:26] Sofia: Thats in line with our expectations. The earlier spreadsheet suggested 15-30% depending on hit rate. What hit rate did you observe?
[01:35] Connor: Hit rate varied by time of day — overall 42% hit rate on the route we tested. Peak hit windows hit 62%. We think with a small change to how you issue the prompts (normalize variable fields) you can push avg to 55-60%.
[01:48] Ben: With higher hit rates does batching still help or is it diminishing?
[01:52] Connor: There's a tradeoff. Batching (we tried micro-batches of 2-4) increases tokens/sec by letting the runtime amortize kernel launch costs. In our experiments batch size 4 gave about +40% tokens/sec, but p95 latency increased from ~320ms to ~470ms on the shorter prompts. So if your SLO is strict at 300ms, batch 4 will break it. For your 400ms p95 target it's borderline.
[02:18] Aisha: Important nuance: batching helps unit economics, but only up to the point where latency SLOs still hold. We recommend route-level policies: enable batching for non-critical routes, keep low-latency routes at batch 1 or 2.
[02:33] [02:40] Marcus: Any changes from quantization? We saw some notes in the deck about 4-bit runs.
[02:44] Connor: Yes, we ran an int4-style quant on the 13B and saw ~1.9x improvement in tokens/sec per dollar for generation-heavy calls, with small delta in output quality on our eval set — roughly 0.6% drop in metric X (the safety/semantic accuracy metric you shared). For short risk scoring prompts that are mostly classification-like, the quality delta looked acceptable. But note some hallucination modes rise a little — recommend more evals if you go quant full-time.
[03:10] Sofia: Could that affect our fraud classification thresholds? We cannot have model drift causing false positives.
[03:15] Connor: Totally—recommend a staged rollout: run quantized model in shadow for 72 hours and compare scores. Also add regression alerts in Redwood Optimize tied to your prompt set.
[03:25] Lina: On the infra side we noticed some p99 spikes mid-morning last run. Could that be autoscaling or cold KV loads?
[03:31] Connor: Probably both. Cold KV cache population will spike backend compute until warm. Also we saw a node-replacement event in the Dedicated cluster during the earlier benchmark which caused a short p99 blip. If you want hard SLOs, Dedicated with reserved capacity is more predictable; hosted will have more variability but lower ops overhead.
[03:49] Marcus: Cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated? Were trying to compare incremental monthly commit vs pay-as-you-go.
[03:56] Aisha: High-level: Dedicated reduces per-token unit costs once you commit and achieve utilization; the spreadsheet simulates commit levels. At ~70% utilization a Dedicated pool gives ~30-40% cheaper per-token compute compared to hosted in our current pricing. But committed costs upfront and requires forecasting.
[04:14] Ben: If we optimize to get higher cache hit rates and batching, that reduces the utilization needed to be cost effective on Dedicated, right?
[04:20] Connor: Exactly. Caching and batching both lower the raw compute per request which means you need fewer GPUs for the same QPS. That shifts the Dedicated breakeven earlier.
[04:29] [04:35] Sofia: What about routing? Could we route lower-priority traffic to cheaper model variants or lower-precision variants?
[04:39] Connor: Yes. Smart routing is one of the quick wins: you can send >90% of less-sensitive requests to a quantized 13B variant and keep a non-quantized model for safety-critical scoring. Redwood supports policy-based routing by route tags and SLA.
[04:52] Marcus: Ok good. Let's talk numbers again — after you enabled prefix cache for route A, tokens/sec per dollar went up 18% overall. Where did the remainder go when you enabled batching?
[05:03] Connor: When we enabled batching across the board (batch 2 for most routes, batch 4 for a couple), combined caching + batching improved tokens/sec per dollar by ~62% versus baseline. But p95 latency for the shortest prompt bucket increased by ~45%. So combined gains look attractive economically, but you need to pick which routes can tolerate the added tail latency.
[05:25] Aisha: And to reiterate, additional wins come from better sequence-length shaping — truncation and forcing shorter max tokens when possible. That reduced average tokens per request by about 12% in the run.
[05:37] Ben: We asked our data team to do trace dumps — Sofia will share sequence length histogram. That should help tune pack and batch config.
[05:43] Sofia: Yes sending that after the call.
[05:45] [06:00] Connor: We also saw some surprising interaction: when batching bumped p95, the retry logic in your client triggered additional requests which negated some benefits. So you might want to increase the client-side timeout to align with expected p95 after batching changes.
[06:12] Lina: Oof, good catch. We'll check client timeouts; currently set to 300ms.
[06:16] Marcus: That explains some doubled requests.
[06:18] Aisha: For next steps we recommended 3 experiments: 1) Run 24h prefix cache validation on the live route, 2) Shadow quantized 13B for 72h, 3) Controlled batching test with batch sizes 2 and then 4 on non-critical route. We'll coordinate timelines.
[06:33] [06:40] Ben: Any doc links?
[06:42] Aisha: Link in chat: pilot-benchmarks.xlsx and the run deck. Also I'll upload a focused cost-model with scenarios for Hosted vs Dedicated with caching assumptions.
[06:52] [07:00] Marcus: Sounds good. A couple quick Qs — does Redwood provide audit logs for cache hits and inference routing? Our compliance folks will want evidence.
[07:07] Connor: Yes, we emit trace-level logs with per-request routing metadata, model variant, cache_hit boolean, and latency. These are available in the Console under the route dashboard and can be exported to your SIEM. For Private deployments we can wire them to your internal logging pipeline.
[07:21] Sofia: Also SSO questions — can we map roles to who can change batching thresholds?
[07:26] Maya: Yes, RBAC supports role-based permissions for route config edits. We can demo that in the next call.
[07:33] [07:40] Marcus: Anything from the competitor angle? We ran a quick bench with Anthropic endpoints and saw slightly better p95 but higher cost per token. It's not a like-for-like.
[07:49] Aisha: Right, and one of our differentiators is the tooling to tie quality alerts to the prompt set so you catch regressions when moving to quant. Anthropic has good safety but different tradeoffs.
[07:59] [08:05] Sofia: Timeline wise — if we want to move to Dedicated for peak traffic in Q3, what should we sign up for now?
[08:11] Aisha: We recommend a 3-month ramp pilot on Hosted with these experiments, then a capacity planning session in mid-June. If the numbers look good we can draft a Dedicated proposal for July start. That gives your ops time to approve budgets.
[08:25] Marcus: Works for us.
[08:28] [08:35] Connor: Quick note on instrumentation: we'll add a dashboard widget for cache hit rate and batching-induced latency per route so you can watch regressions.
[08:44] Ben: Great.
[08:46] [08:55] Aisha: Ok last wrap — I'll send the updated cost model and schedule the latency deep-dive for next Tuesday. Connor will enable prefix cache on Route A and monitor, Sofia will send traces.
[09:04] Marcus: Cool thanks everyone.
[09:06] Aisha: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
